fields.corePath: A NEET repeater opens the site and sees a subject row: Physics, Chemistry, Botany, Zoology. Step 1, he taps one subject — say Physics. Step 2, he picks a chapter from the list, for example Current Electricity, which shows how many past-paper questions sit in it (Current Electricity has 74 from 2013 to 2025). Step 3, he taps Start drill. Step 4, a question comes up one at a time with the year printed next to it and a timer counting up in the corner, four options, and he taps one. Step 5, the answer turns green or red straight away, the solution opens under it, and he taps Next. Step 6, after twenty questions the drill ends and he gets a card: how many right, his average seconds per question against the 105-second NEET budget, and the three questions he took longest on. Step 7, he taps Redo the slow ones, which builds a fresh drill out of only those. No login anywhere in this.
fields.knownGaps: The question bank is 2013 to 2025 for Physics and Chemistry but Botany only goes back to 2017 — I typed those in myself and ran out of evenings. Zoology is complete. Roughly forty questions across all subjects have diagrams that I have as images, and on a narrow phone the image sometimes renders wider than the option list so you have to scroll sideways to see option D. Solutions are text only; for eleven of the harder Physics questions the solution is just the final formula and the answer, not the working, and those are marked with a small "short solution" tag so nobody is surprised. Progress is stored in localStorage, so if he clears his browser or switches from phone to laptop the streak and the slow-question history are gone — there is no account system at all yet. The timer keeps running if he switches tabs, which inflates his average if he goes to check something. Nothing here blocks the drill itself: picking a subject, drilling twenty questions and getting the timing card works on every browser I have tried.

Question 4 of 20      NEET 2019      00:38
A wire of resistance R is stretched to twice its original length without change in volume. The new resistance is
A.  R/2
B.  2R
C.  4R
D.  R/4

Correct. The answer is 4R.
Solution: volume is constant, so doubling the length halves the area. R is proportional to length divided by area, so the resistance goes up by a factor of four.
